It was at Weatherend, a great house full of pictures and treasures, that John Marcher, after many years, found himself face to face again with May Bartram, a woman whose face he half remembered. <break time="0.8s" /> He had the odd impression that their earlier meeting had mattered more than he could recall, and that she, unlike himself, had kept every detail of it alive through all the intervening years. <break time="0.8s" /> He began by recalling that they had met in Rome some eight years before, but she corrected him gently, saying that it had been at Naples, and nearer ten years than eight. <break time="0.8s" /> Then, with a quiet smile, she reminded him of something he had entirely forgotten, namely that during one of those Italian afternoons he had confided to her a strange and deeply private secret. <break time="0.8s" /> He had told her that he had always felt, deep within himself, that something rare and strange, possibly prodigious and terrible, was waiting for him and would sooner or later happen. <break time="0.8s" /> Hearing that she had kept his secret for ten years without sharing it with anyone, Marcher felt, for the first time in his life, that he was no longer entirely alone with it. <break time="0.8s" /> Has it ever happened, she asked, and when he answered that it had not, she listened without a trace of mockery, and soon they agreed to watch for it together.

Some time later, a small inheritance allowed May Bartram to settle in a little house in London, and there Marcher began to visit her regularly, as a man returns to a familiar shelter. <break time="0.8s" /> They often went to the opera together, and in the course of the years their talk returned again and again, sometimes lightly and sometimes gravely, to the thing that lay in wait for him. <break time="0.8s" /> Marcher told himself that a man in his position could not decently marry, for, as he put it, a man of feeling does not ask a lady to accompany him on a tiger hunt. <break time="0.8s" /> The Beast, he believed, was crouching somewhere in the jungle of his days, ready to spring, and it seemed only fair that he alone should face whatever danger its leap might bring. <break time="0.8s" /> Their friends and acquaintances, seeing them so often together, naturally supposed that there was some romance between them, and May allowed this appearance to serve as a screen for the secret that they actually shared. <break time="0.8s" /> I have helped you to pass for a man like another, she once said, and Marcher, grateful for her kindness, never asked himself what this long service might be costing her. <break time="0.8s" /> Year after year he gave her small presents on her birthday, and he congratulated himself on being unselfish, never suspecting that his whole attention, all the while, was fixed upon himself.
